questions.question_text: A recognised risk factor for depression and rapid cycling in bipolar disorder is
questions.explanation: Subclinical hypothyroidism is a risk factor for depression and rapid cycling in bipolar disorder. BAP guidelines (2016) recommend that if rapid cycling poses particular long-term management problems:-       Identify and treat conditions such as hypothyroidism or substance use that may contribute to cycling-       Consider tapering and discontinuing antidepressants that may contribute to cycling-       Track mood states longitudinally and discontinue ineffective treatments to avoid unnecessary polypharmacy Ref: Goodwin GM et al. Evidence-based guidelines for treating bipolar disorder: revised third edition recommendations from the British Association for Psychopharmacology. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2016 Jun;30(6):495-553.

questions.question_text: The male:female ratio of hypothyroidism is
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism is common throughout the world and is particularly common in the UK. Hypothyroidism is approximately ten times more prevalent in women than in men. Ref: Taylor PN et al. Global epidemiology of hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism. Nature Reviews Endocrinology. 2018 May;14(5):301-16.

questions.question_text: Hoover test is a physical examination maneuver done to inform the possible diagnosis of
questions.explanation: Hoover test has been used to differentiate between organic and functional hemiparesis. In conversion disorder (also known as functional neurological symptom disorder in DSM-5 or dissociative neurological symptom disorder in ICD-11), the patient is unable to raise the affected limb from the couch but is able to raise the unaffected limb against resistance, with demonstrable pressing down of the heel on the 'affected' side. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 868.

questions.question_text: Of the following, the clinical feature most suggestive of herpes simplex encephalitis is
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex encephalitis causes fever, somnolence, and delirium (abrupt onset of confusion). In addition, because the virus attacks the temporal lobes and thus damages the limbic system, it routinely causes seizures and amnesia. Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 194.

questions.question_text: A woman who had herpes simplex encephalitis eats excessively, gains weight, and has inappropriately sexual speech. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bilateral temporal lobe damage in some patients with herpes simplex encephalitis may lead to the human variety of Kluver-Bucy syndrome, with manifestations that differ from those seen in monkeys. Only about one-half of humans show any increase in heterosexual activity or masturbation. Mostly only speak in an aggressive or sexually suggestive manner. Showing varieties of oral expression, humans with the syndrome tend to eat excessively and smoke or drink compulsively. Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 194, 372.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about Meige syndrome is correct?

options.text: Idiopathic Meige syndrome has known causes
The manifestations of Meige syndrome are present during sleep
Walking and talking do not alleviate dystonia in Meige syndrome
It is characterised by blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia
Patients are more likely to be middle-aged men than women

correct_answer.text: It is characterised by blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia

correct_answers.text: It is characterised by blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia

questions.explanation: Meige syndrome is a cranial dystonia characterised by the combination of upper and lower cranial involvement and including binocular eyelid spasms (blepharospasm) and involuntary movements of the jaw muscles (oromandibular dystonia). The aetiology and pathogenesis of this extrapyramidal disorder are not well understood. Meige syndrome can be classified into idiopathic, acquired, and inherited subtypes. Inherited forms have proven genetic origin; acquired is due to a known specific cause; idiopathic has unknown causes. Use of the term 'primary' is discouraged. Sleeping, relaxing, talking, pulling the upper eyelid, blowing cheeks, walking, exposure to cold water, yawning, or drinking beverages can all alleviate the dystonia. Meige syndrome is significantly more common in females than males. The male: female ratio is 1:2. The average age of Meige syndrome onset is in the sixth decade. Ref: Ma H et al. Blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia, and meige syndrome: clinical and genetic update. Frontiers in Neurology. 2021 Mar 29;12:630221.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a weak inhibitor of cytochrome P450 enzyme system?
questions.explanation: Citalopram is a weak inhibitor of CYP2D6. Fluoxetine is a moderate-potent inhibitor of CYP2D6 and moderate inhibitor of CYP2C9. Paroxetine and bupropion are potent CYP2D6 inhibitors. Fluvoxamine is a potent inhibitor of CYP1A2 and CYP2C19. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 378-379.

questions.question_text: Some patients intentionally falsify their symptoms and past history, and fabricate signs of physical or mental disorder, with the primary aim of obtaining medical attention and treatment. Which of the following diagnoses is most appropriate in these circumstances?
questions.explanation: In Munchhausen syndrome (factitious disorder imposed on self in ICD-11), patients intentionally falsify their symptoms and past history, and fabricate signs of physical or mental disorder, with the primary aim of obtaining medical attention and treatment. The diagnostic features are the intentional and conscious production of signs, falsification or exaggeration of the history, and the lack of gain beyond medical attention and treatment. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 876.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a risk factor for depression in Parkinson disease?
questions.explanation: Risk factors for depression in Parkinson disease include cognitive impairment, longer disease duration/advanced disease, motor fluctuations, female sex, disability (defined as problems with activities of daily living), higher dose of levodopa, and younger age. Ref: Marinus J et al. Risk factors for non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease. The Lancet Neurology. 2018 Jun 1;17(6):559-68. Ray S, Agarwal P. Depression and anxiety in Parkinson disease. Clinics in geriatric medicine. 2020 Feb 1;36(1):93-104.

questions.question_text: All are true about delirium in palliative care except that delirium

options.text: Occurs in over 50% of patients at some stage in their illness

questions.explanation: Delirium is a common complication encountered during palliative care, occurring in >50% of cases. Patients may become agitated or aggressive, or may present with hypoactive delirium (e.g. lethargy, somnolence). The cause of delirium is frequently multifactorial. Antipsychotics may reduce the severity and duration of delirium but may also further cloud the patient's mental state. Ref: Aziz VM, Saeed R. Palliative care for older people: the psychiatrist's role. BJPsych Advances. 2019 Jan;25(1):37-46. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 854.

questions.question_text: Poor prognostic factors with respect to recovery following traumatic brain injury include all except

options.text: Long duration of loss of consciousness
Focal damage restricted to the non-dominant lobe

correct_answer.text: Focal damage restricted to the non-dominant lobe

correct_answers.text: Focal damage restricted to the non-dominant lobe

questions.explanation: Factors associated with poorer long-term outcome after traumatic brain injury include the conscious level post-injury; duration of loss of consciousness; increased duration of post-traumatic amnesia (>24 hours, poorer outcome); age (older has poorer prognosis); pre-injury educational or occupational level; and reduced pre-injury cognitive reserve (e.g. due to cerebrovascular disease or alcohol dependence). Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 854.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y suffers from psychiatric symptoms such as apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, and depressed mood. He reports severe weakness and abdominal pain. On examination you discover unexplained dark skin pigmentation. This should suggest
questions.explanation: Addison disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) is characterised by chronic glucocorticoid and/or mineralocorticoid deficiency due to failure of the adrenal cortex. It should be suspected in all acutely or chronically ill patients with general fatigue or severe weakness and unexplained dehydration, hypotension, weight loss, fever, abdominal pain, and hyperpigmentation. Key lab characteristics are hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and (especially in children) hypoglycaemia. Psychiatric symptoms include apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, and depressed mood. Ref: Barthel A et al. An update on Addison's disease. Experimental and Clinical Endocrinology & Diabetes. 2019 Feb;127(02/03):165-75.

questions.question_text: The term 'worried well'

options.text: Describes a clearly defined group of patients
Is only used to describe healthy patients

questions.explanation: The term 'worried well' usually describes a group of patients who are perceived as using health services inappropriately or disproportionately, when other more deserving patients should be given attention. The term suggests that these patients are well. However, research has shown that only 14% of those who frequently present without clear physical findings have a somatisation disorder while 86% have organic disease or minor acute illness. The term has never been properly defined, and the 'worried well' are not a clearly defined group. Increasingly, it has been recognised that the term 'worried well' is potentially patronising, unprofessional, disrespectful, and doctor-centred. Ref: Gray DP et al. The worried well. British Journal of General Practice. 2020 Feb 1;70(691):84-5.

questions.question_text: Persons with HIV/AIDS have a significantly greater risk of developing depressive disorders than the general population. Which of the following factors is NOT associated with these higher rates of depressive disorders in seropositive individuals?

options.text: Direct brain damage by the virus

questions.explanation: Several factors related to HIV/AIDS status contribute to higher rates of depressive disorders in seropositive individuals than in the general population. These factors may be divided into three groups: (1) infection-immunological factors, including biological abnormalities that result either from direct damage caused by HIV (e.g. direct brain damage by the virus) or from increased inflammatory response to HIV (e.g. prolonged inflammation, hypogonadism leading to low testosterone in men); (2) psychosocial factors encompassing human interactions and subjective experiences (e.g. chronic life stressors, stigma, social isolation); and (3) exogenous factors including medications (e.g. anti-retroviral therapy (ART) and other medications) and addictive substances. Among ART agents, efavirenz has been most commonly implicated in contributing to depressive symptoms. Moreover, the recently developed integrase inhibitors (such as dolutegravir, elvitegravir, and raltegravir) have also been linked to higher rates of depressive symptoms. There is no notable association between genetic risk and comorbid depression in people with HIV. Ref: Medeiros GC et al. Depressive disorders in HIV/AIDS: a clinically focused narrative review. Harvard review of psychiatry. 2020 May 1;28(3):146-58.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has the best evidence for use in HIV-associated dementia (HAD)?
questions.explanation: The mainstay of treatment for HIV-associated dementia (HAD) is the suppression of virus replication in the brain (i.e. anti-retroviral therapy or ART). Although the introduction of ART has reduced the incidence and prevalence of HAD, the incidence and prevalence of milder forms of HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) have not reduced over recent years. No clinical trial of neuroprotective adjuvant therapies (e.g. lithium, cholinesterase inhibitors, selegiline, minocycline) has illustrated robust cognitive benefits in HAND and thus no adjuvant therapies are currently in routine clinical use. Ref: Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. pp. 374-375. Sharma I. Interrogating the impact of combination antiretroviral therapies on HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders. HIV medicine. 2021 Oct;22(9):783-90.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a direct effect of HIV on the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: Although HIV is notorious for its devastating impact on the cellular immune system, it also instigates direct pathology in the central nervous system, culminating in a group of syndromes of impaired cognition and functionality, known collectively as HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND). HIV-associated dementia (HAD) is the most severe form of HAND. Direct effects of HIV on the CNS include aseptic meningitis, HAND, and vacuolar myelopathy. Opportunistic infections include cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, tuberculous meningitis, and neurosyphilis. CNS lymphoma is considered to be secondary to ineffective immunoregulation of Epstein-Barr virus. Ref: Sharma I. Interrogating the impact of combination antiretroviral therapies on HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders. HIV medicine. 2021 Oct;22(9):783-90. Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. pp. 374-375.

questions.question_text: What is the most common psychiatric condition in HIV-positive individuals?
questions.explanation: Depression is the most prevalent psychiatric illness in HIV-positive individuals. Ref: Knights MJ et al. HIV infection and its psychiatric manifestations: a clinical overview. BJPsych Advances. 2017 Jul;23(4):265-77. Rein SM et al. Causes of hospitalisation among a cohort of people with HIV from a London centre followed from 2011 to 2018. BMC infectious diseases. 2021 Apr 29;21(1):395.

questions.question_text: A 34 year old homosexual man with a history of IV drug use presents with forgetfulness, loss of concentration, and mental slowing. He appears clumsy and apathetic. Which of the following statements is false with regard to his condition?

options.text: Laboratory evidence of HIV infection is necessary to make the diagnosis
Aphasia, agnosia and apraxia are unusual
Decline in motor function may be present
The minimum duration of symptoms must be 1 year to make the diagnosis
Decline in memory may not be severe enough to impair all ADLs

correct_answer.text: The minimum duration of symptoms must be 1 year to make the diagnosis

correct_answers.text: The minimum duration of symptoms must be 1 year to make the diagnosis

questions.explanation: Cortical dementias consist of illnesses in which neuropsychologic signs of cortical dysfunction – typically aphasia, agnosia, and apraxia – accompany dementia. Because the brain's subcortical areas are relatively untouched, patients remain alert, attentive, and ambulatory. Alzheimer disease serves as the prime example of a cortical dementia. In contrast, subcortical dementias are typified by affective change, and slowed mental processing, which overshadow cognitive impairment. Gait abnormalities constitute the other core feature. Prime examples are Parkinson disease, NPH, HIV-associated dementia (HAD), vascular cognitive impairment, and MS. Because HAD develops rapidly – over several weeks to a few months – it is considered a rapidly progressive dementia. Psychomotor retardation, loss of dexterity, and gait impairment are so characteristic that HAD is considered a prime example of subcortical dementia. HAD patients initially remain verbal and articulate. Later, reticence, apathy, and withdrawal predominate. Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 115, 134.

questions.question_text: The most common neuropsychiatric symptom associated with Parkinson disease (PD) is
questions.explanation: While depression may be partly reactive to receiving the diagnosis or experiencing a worsening of PD symptoms, the depressive illness may be due to the actual disease process itself. Depression in PD is very frequent (50%) and is more common in women and is often atypical in nature. Impulse control disorders include addiction-related behaviours such as binge eating, pathological gambling, compulsive shopping or abnormal sexual behaviours. Epidemiological studies suggest 13-29% of patients having at least one impulse control disorder (see Dujardin et al., 2020 for a review). Ref: Jones S, Torsney KM, Scourfield L, Berryman K, Henderson EJ. Neuropsychiatric symptoms in Parkinson's disease: aetiology, diagnosis and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2020 Nov;26(6):333-42. Dujardin K, Sgambato V. Neuropsychiatric disorders in parkinson's disease: what do we know about the role of dopaminergic and non-dopaminergic systems?. Frontiers in neuroscience. 2020 Jan 29;14:25.

questions.question_text: In patients with transient global amnesia, the amnesic episode resolves within
questions.explanation: The fundamental clinical feature of transient global amnesia (TGA) is the acute onset of amnesia. During an attack, patients cannot memorise or learn new information, that is, they have anterograde amnesia. They also cannot recall information acquired very recently, such as the events in the last several hours or days (i.e., they also have retrograde amnesia). Most patients seem calm but bewildered. TGA lasts for 3 to 24 hours but is most severe during the initial 1-2 hours. By definition, the total duration must not exceed 24 hours. Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 113.

questions.question_text: Which of the following treatments for multiple sclerosis is most likely to lead to depression?
questions.explanation: Steroid treatment of multiple sclerosis (MS) - as with steroid treatment of lupus, organ transplant rejection, and inflammatory bowel disease – can induce not only mania and a thought disorder, but also depressive symptoms. Although ultimately unsubstantiated, initial reports indicated that interferons used to treat MS caused or exacerbated depression in MS patients. The role of interferon-beta in the aetiology of MS depression is unclear, but it is now thought that depression occurs no more frequently in people treated with interferon-beta. Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 352. Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 808.

questions.question_text: In the treatment of post-stroke depression, antidepressants should be continued for
questions.explanation: People with post-stroke depression who are treated with antidepressant medication should be monitored for adverse effects and treated for at least 4 months beyond initial recovery. It is generally advised to continue antidepressants for 4-6 months, followed by gradual withdrawal of the drug. Ref: Bowen A et al. Royal College of Physicians 2016 National clinical guideline for stroke. RCP. Sarkar A et al. Post-stroke depression: Chaos to exposition. Brain research bulletin. 2021 Mar 1;168:74-88.

questions.question_text: Regarding the prevention of post-stroke depression, which of the following is true?

options.text: SSRIs should always be prescribed for the prevention of post-stroke depression
There is no formal indication for prophylactic antidepressant use in post-stroke depression
Psychosocial interventions are highly effective in preventing post-stroke depression
Tricyclic antidepressants should always be prescribed for the prevention of post-stroke depression
Antidepressants and psychosocial interventions have proven useless in the prevention of post-stroke depression

correct_answer.text: There is no formal indication for prophylactic antidepressant use in post-stroke depression

correct_answers.text: There is no formal indication for prophylactic antidepressant use in post-stroke depression

questions.explanation: Given conflicting and limited evidence, there is currently no formal indication for prophylactic antidepressant use in post-stroke depression. Some of the main limitations with studies that have investigated prophylactic interventions are high dropout rates and narrow enrollment criteria, leading to samples that may not have been representative of real-world populations. Additional and more inclusive studies are needed to formally determine the efficacy, cost-effectiveness, and optimal timing of pharmacological and psychosocial interventions in preventing post-stroke depression. Ref: Medeiros GC et al. Post-stroke depression: a 2020 updated review. General hospital psychiatry. 2020 Sep 1;66:70-80.

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old woman has a history of 2 episodes of unilateral blindness that each lasted for a few weeks. She now has paraesthesia of the left leg and is clinically depressed. Her MRI brain shows multiple demyelinating plaques. With respect to her depression, which of the following is NOT correct?

options.text: It can be treated with SSRIs
There is a lifetime prevalence of up to 50% in those with the same neurological condition
It can be treated with cognitive behavioural therapy
It has been associated with some drugs used to treat the neurological condition

questions.explanation: Depression is common in people with multiple sclerosis (MS), with a lifetime prevalence of up to 50%. Disease-modifying treatments used in MS that are associated with depression include daclizumab, alemtuzumab, and natalizumab. SSRIs should be first-line treatment for depression in MS. CBT is the most appropriate psychological intervention with the best efficacy in comparison to supportive therapy or usual care. ECT can be considered for those who are actively suicidal or severely depressed and at high risk. ECT may trigger an exacerbation of MS symptoms, although some studies suggest that no neurological disturbance occurs. ECT is not absolutely contraindicated in MS. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 808-809.

questions.question_text: Which of the following types of memory remains intact in amnestic disorders?
questions.explanation: The central symptom of amnestic disorders is the development of a memory disorder characterised by impairment in the ability to learn new information (anterograde amnesia) and an inability to recall previously remembered knowledge (retrograde amnesia). Short-term and recent memory are usually impaired. Overlearned information or remote events usually remain intact, but there can be amnesia for even the less remote past (over the past decade). Immediate memory (tested, for example, by asking a patient to repeat six numbers) remains intact. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 245-246.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding cognitive impairment seen in multiplesclerosis (MS)?

options.text: It is no more common than in the general population
It can be explained by the increased prevalence of depression in MS
A subcortical dementia can develop late in the illness
It is best screened for using the Mini-Mental State Examination

correct_answer.text: A subcortical dementia can develop late in the illness

correct_answers.text: A subcortical dementia can develop late in the illness

questions.explanation: Cognitive impairment is present in 40-70% of people with multiple sclerosis (MS). Most people experience mild-moderate cognitive impairment. A decline in IQ from estimated premorbid levels has been documented and impairment can be detected across many cognitive domains. Information processing and working memory are impaired early and more severely than would be expected from general cognitive blunting. For these reasons, tests of processing speed (e.g. Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test or PASAT) are used to screen for cognitive impairment. Cognitive performance may be influenced by fatigue and depression. Data suggest that disease-modifying therapies have a beneficial effect on cognition. Initially reported benefits of donepezil have NOT been replicated, and there is no evidence that memantine or rivastigmine have enhancing cognitive properties in people with MS. MS produces a subcortical dementia that appears late in the course of the illness, long after physical disabilities have developed. Ref: Ron MA. The neuropsychiatry of multiple sclerosis. BJPsych Advances. 2018 May;24(3):178-87. Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 349.

questions.question_text: With respect to the management of Parkinson disease (PD), which of the following is correct?

options.text: Any cholinesterase inhibitor can be used in PD dementia, as RCT evidence is abundant
Hypomania is a potential side effect of levodopa
Clozapine must be avoided in PD psychosis
PD psychosis is associated with decreases in antiparkinsonian medications
Quetiapine is best avoided in PD psychosis

correct_answer.text: Hypomania is a potential side effect of levodopa

correct_answers.text: Hypomania is a potential side effect of levodopa

questions.explanation: Hypomania is a psychiatric side effect that can be caused by levodopa. Risk factors for the development of psychosis in Parkinson disease (PD) include the duration and severity of illness, cognitive impairment, and treatment with dopaminergic and anticholinergic medications. If intervention is warranted for psychosis in PD, rivastigmine has good efficacy in those with cognitive impairment. NICE guidelines advocate low-dose quetiapine and clozapine as the most appropriate medications in PD psychosis. The only drug currently licensed for the treatment of PD dementia is rivastigmine, with memantine as second line if patient is intolerant to rivastigmine. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 918. Jones S et al. Neuropsychiatric symptoms in Parkinson's disease: aetiology, diagnosis and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-10.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of depression in epilepsy is
questions.explanation: Depression is the most common psychiatric comorbidity in people with epilepsy. Prevalence ranges from 10% in people with well-controlled epilepsy to 50% for those with refractory and symptomatic focal epilepsy. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 138. Mula M et al. Psychiatric comorbidities in people with epilepsy. Neurology: Clinical Practice. 2020 May 28. Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 785.

questions.question_text: Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) are suspected in a 42-year-old mansuffering from poorly controlled epilepsy. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: PNES are more common in males
Prolactin levels are elevated after a PNES
Video EEG is the gold standard for diagnosing PNES
Known epileptic patients do not have PNES
The presence of depression highly suggests PNES

correct_answer.text: Video EEG is the gold standard for diagnosing PNES

correct_answers.text: Video EEG is the gold standard for diagnosing PNES

questions.explanation: The most common demographic for psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) is young adult women. Approximately 10% of patients with PNES also have epilepsy, but their coexistence is approximately 30% in patients with intellectual disability. Patients with epilepsy and PNES can be particularly difficult to treat if they are unable to distinguish between their epileptic and nonepileptic seizures. Video EEG is the gold standard for diagnosing PNES. Certain lab findings can support a diagnosis of PNES but do not replace the EEG. Prolactin should be elevated two to three times its baseline level after a convulsive epileptic seizure but will not be elevated after a PNES. About half of the patients with PNES have concurrent depression, but depression is also quite common in the epilepsy population. Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 229-230.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs is particularly epileptogenic and should be used with caution in epilepsy and psychosis?
questions.explanation: Clozapine is the most epileptogenic antipsychotic. In people with epilepsy, seizure aggravation can be seen even at low doses. However, clozapine has been used successfully in people with epilepsy stable on antiseizure medications without worsening seizures and even in treatment-resistant epilepsy. Clozapine is considered higher risk and care is required during its use in people with epilepsy. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 790. Mula M et al. Psychiatric comorbidities in people with epilepsy. Neurology: Clinical Practice. 2020 May 28.

questions.question_text: Post-traumatic epilepsy is seen in what proportion of patients with open head injury?
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) occurs in 5% of closed and 30% of open head injuries, usually during the first year, and worsens prognosis. PTE remits in only 25% to 50% of cases. PTE usually takes the form of focal seizures with impaired awareness (previously named complex partial seizures) that undergo secondary generalisation. Not only does PTE cause disability and carry the risk of further head injury, but anti-epileptic drugs may also exacerbate TBI-induced cognitive and personality changes. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 173. Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 555.

questions.question_text: Post-concussion syndrome is characterized by all except
questions.explanation: Post-concussion syndrome is characterised by one or more core symptoms – headache, memory impairment, and insomnia – lasting more than 2 to 3 months after a head injury. These and other symptoms of post-concussion syndrome – including irritability, sleepiness, tinnitus – remain entirely subjective and often nonspecific, variable, and occasionally unending. Patients with post-concussion syndrome characteristically describe mild amnesia accompanied by inattention or easy distractibility, slowed information processing, and difficulty completing complex mental tasks. Post-concussion syndrome patients also often report dizziness. Patients also commonly have exquisite sensitivity to light (photophobia) and sound (phonophobia). In addition, patients often describe symptoms of depression, anxiety, irritability, and moodiness. Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 559-560.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is false about mania seen in multiple sclerosis?

options.text: It is more common than in the general population
There is predominant frontal distribution of plaques on MRI
It can be induced by treatments prescribed for multiple sclerosis
It can occur as part of the primary neurological disorder
Mood stabilisers are an appropriate treatment option

correct_answer.text: There is predominant frontal distribution of plaques on MRI

correct_answers.text: There is predominant frontal distribution of plaques on MRI

questions.explanation: The incidence of bipolar disorder can be as high as 13% in the multiple sclerosis (MS) population, compared with 1-6% in the general population. There is a particular predisposition to mania and hypomania in MS patients. Occult inflammatory processes may be responsible for symptoms in this population. Mania can also be induced by drugs such as steroids or baclofen. MS patients presenting with mania may be treated with mood stabilisers such as sodium valproate, as these are better tolerated than lithium (which can cause diuresis and thus lead to difficulties with tolerance in people with bladder disorder; and may be poorly tolerated in some patients due to sedation, especially in patients prone to falls). No studies have systematically examined the relationship between plaque location and the presence of manic symptoms, perhaps due to the inconsistent relationship between plaque location and neurological deficits in MS. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 810. Satzer D, Bond DJ. Mania secondary to focal brain lesions: implications for understanding the functional neuroanatomy of bipolar disorder. Bipolar disorders. 2016 May;18(3):205-20.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man with a recent history of stroke is admitted to the medical unit. A psychiatric opinion is requested due to his deteriorating mental state. His MRI brain shows lesions proximal to the left frontal lobe. Which of the following psychiatric conditions is most likely to occur in this scenario?
questions.explanation: People with left cerebral hemisphere infarction have a higher disposition to develop depression after stroke. Individuals with left hemispheric lesions in the vicinity of frontal and basal ganglia are more prone to depression and cognitive deficits as compared to the right hemisphere. In analogy to the monoaminergic hypothesis of depression, post-stroke depression could be related to the interruption induced by ischaemic lesion(s) of the amine-containing axons ascending from the brainstem to the left cerebral cortex. This would lead to reduced synthesis of serotonin and norepinephrine in the limbic areas of frontal and temporal lobes and basal ganglia. Ref: Rizvi S et al. Post Stroke Psychiatric Syndromes. Psychol Behav Sci Int J. 2018;9(5):1-4. Sarkar A et al. Post-stroke depression: Chaos to exposition. Brain research bulletin. 2021 Mar 1;168:74-88. Villa RF et al. Post-stroke depression: mechanisms and pharmacological treatment. Pharmacology & therapeutics. 2018 Apr 1;184:131-44.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications used in the treatment of multiple sclerosis has NOT been associated with the induction of mania?
questions.explanation: Steroid treatment in multiple sclerosis (MS) patients may cause a moderate degree of mania. Patients with a family history of alcohol use disorder or other affective disorder are more vulnerable to this. Other medications, such as tizanidine, baclofen, and dantrolene, can also cause hypo/mania. Manic symptoms due to medication are often dose-dependent and manifest soon after initiating the medication. In the case of medication-induced mania, cessation or dosage reduction is recommended whenever possible. Ref: Yang S, Wichser L. Manic episode in patient with bipolar disorder and recent multiple sclerosis diagnosis: a case report. Medicine. 2020 Oct 10;99(42). Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 810. Satzer D, Bond DJ. Mania secondary to focal brain lesions: implications for understanding the functional neuroanatomy of bipolar disorder. Bipolar disorders. 2016 May;18(3):205-20.

questions.question_text: A psychiatric trainee is keen to obtain prolactin concentrations from a patient to determine possibility of epileptic seizure activity. What is the time frame after a seizure within which the measurements must be taken?
questions.explanation: Prolactin should be elevated two to three times its baseline level after a convulsive epileptic seizure (but will not be elevated after a psychogenic nonepileptic seizure). However, because this abnormality is short-lived, blood for the test must be drawn 10-20 minutes after the seizure and a baseline for comparison is also necessary. Prolactin is less likely to be elevated after a focal impaired awareness seizure or a frontal lobe seizure. Note that dopamine antagonists, tricyclic antidepressants, and syncope can also elevate the prolactin level. Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 229.

questions.question_text: What is the lifetime prevalence of depression in patients with multiple sclerosis?
questions.explanation: Depression is common in people with multiple sclerosis (MS), with a lifetime prevalence of up to 50%. SSRIs should be first-line treatment for depression in MS. CBT is the most appropriate psychological intervention with the best efficacy in comparison to supportive therapy or usual care. ECT can be considered for those who are actively suicidal or severely depressed and at high risk. ECT may trigger an exacerbation of MS symptoms, although some studies suggest that no neurological disturbance occurs. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 808-809.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man with Parkinson disease presents with psychotic symptoms characterised by paranoia and visual hallucinations. His wife does not want his anti-parkinsonian medication to be stopped, as discontinuation has worsened the motor features of his Parkinson disease in the past. Of the following, which antipsychotic would be most appropriate choice?
questions.explanation: The initial management of Parkinson disease (PD) psychosis involves the identification and treatment of any precipitating factors. Psychosis may be the manifestation of an acute illness or a change in medication. If intervention is warranted, rivastigmine has good efficacy in those with cognitive impairment. Clozapine and pimavanserin are efficacious. NICE guidelines advocate low-dose quetiapine and clozapine as the most appropriate medications in PD psychosis. Ref: Jones S et al. Neuropsychiatric symptoms in Parkinson's disease: aetiology, diagnosis and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-10.

questions.question_text: The gene for Huntington disease (HD) is located on which chromosome?
questions.explanation: Huntington disease (HD) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system with genetic autosomal dominant inheritance. HD results from expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT (huntingtin) gene on the short arm of chromosome 4. Alleles with 40 or more repeats are fully penetrant. Ref: Kumar A et al. Therapeutic Advances for Huntington's Disease. Brain Sciences. 2020 Jan;10(1):43. Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington's Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.

questions.question_text: Traumatic brain injury may predispose to the development of
questions.explanation: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) and especially repeated mild TBI can initiate long-term neurodegeneration processes leading to pathological features that have similarities with Alzheimer disease. Ref: Ramos-Cejudo J et al. Traumatic brain injury and Alzheimer's disease: the cerebrovascular link. EBioMedicine. 2018 Feb 1;28:21-30.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y has a history of epilepsy and psychosis. He currently remains psychotic. Of the following, the most appropriate drug of choice is
questions.explanation: Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 790.

questions.question_text: The psychiatric syndrome that occurs most commonly after a stroke is
questions.explanation: The development of depression after a stroke (post-stroke depression) is the most frequent and burdensome neuropsychiatric post-stroke complication. Ref: Medeiros GC et al. Post-stroke depression: a 2020 updated review. General hospital psychiatry. 2020 Sep 1;66:70-80.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Z has a history of epilepsy and has now been diagnosed with depression. Which class of drugs should be used as first a line treatment in her case?
questions.explanation: SSRIs are recommended in people with epilepsy. SSRIs may be anticonvulsant at therapeutic doses but pro-convulsant in overdose. SSRIs with the lowest risk of interactions with antiseizure medications are generally preferred. Citalopram/escitalopram and sertraline are usually considered first-line treatments for depression in the context of epilepsy. Escitalopram is preferred over citalopram due to a lower risk of seizures in overdose. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 789. Mula M et al. Psychiatric comorbidities in people with epilepsy. Neurology: Clinical Practice. 2020 May 28.

questions.question_text: Lesions caused by a traumatic injury to which part of the brain are associated with depression?
questions.explanation: Biological factors associated with depressive symptoms after traumatic brain injury (TBI) include:-       Dorsolateral and ventromedial prefrontal cortical lesions in the left frontal lobe-       Intellectual impairment-       Comorbid anxiety-       Aggressive behaviour-       Prolonged syndromal major depression in the pre-TBI period Ref: Roy D et al. Risk factors for new-onset depression after first-time traumatic brain injury. Psychosomatics. 2018 Jan 1;59(1):47-57.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a risk factor for cognitive impairment in Parkinson disease (PD)?
questions.explanation: Risk factors for cognitive impairment and dementia in Parkinson disease (PD) include hallucinations, older age, overall severity of motor impairment, speech impairment, older age at onset of PD, bradykinesia severity, axial impairment, low level of education, depression, and male sex. Ref: Marinus J et al. Risk factors for non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease. The Lancet Neurology. 2018 Jun 1;17(6):559-68. Jones S et al. Neuropsychiatric symptoms in Parkinson's disease: aetiology, diagnosis and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-10.

questions.question_text: Concerning movement disorders in Parkinson disease (PD), all are true except

options.text: Medication used to treat PD may affect psychiatric symptoms
Movement disorders in PD may mask depression
Parkinsonism may be aggravated by psychotropic medication
Levodopa can cause dose dependent psychiatric manifestations
The presence of cognitive impairment improves prognosis in PD

correct_answer.text: The presence of cognitive impairment improves prognosis in PD

correct_answers.text: The presence of cognitive impairment improves prognosis in PD

questions.explanation: Hypomimia (lack of facial expression) in Parkinson disease (PD) can mask depression and make it more difficult to diagnose. Dopaminergic agents used in PD may cause significant adverse effects, such as dyskinesias, sleep disturbances, visual hallucinations, thought disorders, and other mental status changes. Levodopa can cause psychiatric side effects including visual hallucinations, depression, hypomania, sleep disturbances, abnormal dreams, cognitive impairment, agitation, psychosis, and delirium. Typical and most atypical antipsychotic agents – because to a greater or lesser degree they all block D2 receptors – routinely cause and/or exacerbate parkinsonism. Cognitive impairment in PD is associated with increased disability, mortality, carer burden, and nursing home placement. Ref: Jones S et al. Neuropsychiatric symptoms in Parkinson's disease: aetiology, diagnosis and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-10. Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 423-426. Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 918.

questions.question_text: Huntington disease is transmitted through which of the following genetic changes?

options.text: Autosomal recessive gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
Autosomal dominant gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
Autosomal recessive gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
Autosomal dominant gene on the long arm of chromosome 4
X-linked recessive gene on the short arm of chromosome 4

correct_answer.text: Autosomal dominant gene on the short arm of chromosome 4

correct_answers.text: Autosomal dominant gene on the short arm of chromosome 4

questions.explanation: Huntington disease (HD) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system with genetic autosomal dominant inheritance. HD results from expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT (huntingtin) gene on the short arm of chromosome 4. Alleles with 40 or more repeats are fully penetrant. Ref: Kumar A et al. Therapeutic Advances for Huntington's Disease. Brain Sciences. 2020 Jan;10(1):43. Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington's Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum recommended dose of valproate to be given to pregnant women with bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation: Valproate confers a high risk (around 10% for major malformations) and should not be used in women of child-bearing age except where all other treatment has failed. NICE recommends against the use of valproate in pregnancy. Valproate should be discontinued before a woman becomes pregnant. Women taking valproate who are planning a pregnancy should be advised to gradually stop the drug because of the high risk of foetal malformations and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes after any exposure in pregnancy. If valproate is the only drug that works for a particular woman, and this is seen as the only option for her during pregnancy, then she needs to be given a clear briefing of the risks and to sign a consent form confirming that she understands the risk of malformations and developmental delays. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 690-692.

questions.question_text: When used as mood stabilizers, what is the minimum period suggested to withdraw anticonvulsant drugs?
questions.explanation: It is not known if the abrupt discontinuation of anticonvulsants (such as valproate and carbamazepine) worsens the natural course of bipolar illness in the same way that discontinuation of lithium does. Until further data are available, it is recommended that anticonvulsants should be discontinued slowly, over at least a month. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 260, 266.

questions.question_text: What is the lifetime risk of suicide in Huntington disease?
questions.explanation: Suicidal ideation and attempts are common in Huntington disease (HD) and correlate with family history of suicide, a history of previous attempts, and the presence of depression, especially in prodromal stages. At a higher rate than in other neurodegenerative illnesses, up to 10% of individuals who are carriers or have overt signs of HD end their lives by suicide. They tend to have had depression or anxiety, aggression, impaired judgment, or impetuous behaviour – alone or in combination. Ref: Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington's Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710. Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 429-430.

questions.question_text: What is the most common behavioural change observed in patients with Huntington disease?
questions.explanation: The high prevalence of behavioural problems in patients with Huntington disease was first recorded by Craufurd et al. in 2001. The most common behavioural change observed in patients with Huntington disease is lack of initiative followed by poor judgement, blunting of affect, poor self-care, self-centeredness and inflexibility. Irritability, impulsivity and verbal outbursts are also reported ranging from 15 to 60% of cases. Ref: Craufurd D Thompson JC Snowden (2001); behavioral change in Huntington's disease. Neuropsychiatry and behavioral neurology; 14: 219-226 Abdollah Zadegan S, et al. Frequency and Pathophysiology of Apathy in Huntington Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. The Journal of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences. 2022 Nov 10: https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.neuropsych.20220033

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is more associated with Huntington disease dementia rather than Alzheimer dementia?

options.text: Impairment in executive function correlates with general cognitive decline

questions.explanation: Cortical dementias consist of illnesses in which neuropsychologic signs of cortical dysfunction – typically aphasia, agnosia, and apraxia – accompany dementia. Because the brain's subcortical areas are relatively untouched, patients remain alert, attentive, and ambulatory. Alzheimer disease serves as the prime example of a cortical dementia. In contrast, subcortical dementias are typified by affective change, and slowed mental processing, which overshadow cognitive impairment. Gait abnormalities constitute the other core feature. People with HD develop subcortical dementia, with slowing, apathy, and amnesia. Poor memory, impaired planning ability, and faulty judgment, especially in financial matters, characterise their dementia. Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 115, 429. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 166.

questions.question_text: Choose the accurate statement regarding depression in terminal illness.

options.text: The presence of somatic symptoms strongly favours the diagnosis
Depression does not respond to antidepressants
Depression is uncommon in palliative care settings

questions.explanation: Depression is commonly encountered in palliative care patients. However, diagnostic challenges include the fact that neurovegetative symptoms of depression (anergia, fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, impaired concentration, sleep disturbance) are also common manifestations of advanced medical illness. Somatic symptoms are not useful when diagnosing depression in such cases. Pervasive global anhedonia is a more useful criterion for the diagnosis of depression. Dying patients may also underreport or consciously disguise depressive symptoms in their final weeks of life. Treatment of depression in this setting includes SSRIs, SNRIs, low dose amitriptyline (avoid in those with higher risk of delirium; useful if neuropathic pain is present), and lofepramine. Rapid-acting psychostimulants (e.g. dexamphetamine, methylphenidate, methylamphetamine, and pemoline) may be useful in patients with a short life expectancy. The improved risk-benefit ratio of SSRIs and SNRIs make it important to recognise and treat depressive symptoms. Ref: Aziz VM, Saeed R. Palliative care for older people: the psychiatrist's role. BJPsych Advances. 2019 Jan;25(1):37-46.

questions.question_text: Which of the following tests would be required to make a diagnosis of Huntington disease in a patient without a family history?
questions.explanation: Physicians can base a preliminary diagnosis of Huntington disease on a patient's having chorea, dementia, and a relative with a similar disorder. Readily available DNA testing for patients and potential carriers, including a fetus, can confirm or exclude the diagnosis. Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 430.

questions.question_text: Mr. P has treatment-resistant schizophrenia and is currently on clozapine 600mg/day. Which anticonvulsant is advised for the prevention of clozapine-induced seizures?
questions.explanation: To prevent clozapine-induced seizures, consider prophylactic topiramate, lamotrigine, gabapentin, or valproate if the patient is on high dose clozapine (>500mg/day) or with high plasma level (>500micrograms/L). Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 213.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about periodic limb movements and periodic limb movement disorder (PLMD) is correct?

options.text: The diagnosis of PLMD is made by genetic testing
Periodic limb movements occur during sleep
People with PLMD experience restorative sleep
Periodic limb movements are a subtype of tics

correct_answer.text: Periodic limb movements occur during sleep

correct_answers.text: Periodic limb movements occur during sleep

questions.explanation: Periodic limb movements during sleep (PLMS) are involuntary, sleep-related phenomena characterised by periodic episodes of repetitive, stereotypical movements of the limbs. They are common in adults over 60 years of age (approximately 34%). They may be a feature in up to 15% of patients with insomnia. The diagnosis of periodic limb movement disorder (PLMD) is a diagnosis of exclusion. For PLMD to be established, other sleep disorders associated with PLMS need to be excluded: namely restless legs syndrome, narcolepsy, REM sleep behaviour disorder, and sleep-related breathing disorder. Moreover, PLMS should be linked to sleep complaints and/or daytime impairment. Patients with PLMD commonly report non-restorative sleep, excessive daytime sleepiness, and poor concentration and work performance. Polysomnography may aid in diagnosis. Ref: Drakatos P et al. Periodic limb movements during sleep: a narrative review. Journal of Thoracic Disease. 2021 Nov;13(11):6476. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 475.

questions.question_text: Many patients with chronic fatigue syndrome meet the criteria for psychiatric diagnoses, most commonly
questions.explanation: Many patients with chronic fatigue syndrome meet the criteria for psychiatric diagnoses, most commonly major depression. Many patients resist a 'psychiatric' diagnosis, attributing mood disturbance to the restriction on activities caused by illness. Despite this, treatment of co-morbid depressive or anxiety symptoms can produce clinical improvement. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 875.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old man with Parkinson disease develops psychosis unrelated to levodopa use. Of the following antipsychotics, the most appropriate choice for his treatment is
questions.explanation: The initial management of Parkinson disease (PD) psychosis involves the identification and treatment of any precipitating factors. Psychosis may be the manifestation of an acute illness or a change in medication. If intervention is warranted, rivastigmine has good efficacy in those with cognitive impairment. Clozapine and pimavanserin are efficacious. NICE guidelines advocate low-dose quetiapine and clozapine as the most appropriate medications in PD psychosis. Ref: Jones S et al. Neuropsychiatric symptoms in Parkinson's disease: aetiology, diagnosis and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-10.

questions.question_text: Which of the following factors has been implicated in the pathophysiological processes of restless legs syndrome?
questions.explanation: The role of iron deficiency in the pathophysiological processes of restless legs syndrome (RLS) is recognised. 25% of RLS patients have iron deficiency, and 43% of iron deficient patients experience symptoms of leg restlessness. Moreover, RLS symptom severity is associated with low-normal range of serum ferritin. Conversely, the role of iron deficiency in periodic limb movements without RLS remains largely unexplored, despite its well-established role in RLS with periodic limb movements during sleep. Ref: Drakatos P et al. Periodic limb movements during sleep: a narrative review. Journal of Thoracic Disease. 2021 Nov;13(11):6476.

questions.question_text: How does the safety of lamotrigine in pregnancy compare to the safety of valproate or carbamazepine in pregnancy?

options.text: Lamotrigine carries a greater risk of major malformations
Lamotrigine is safer than valproate, but not safer than carbamazepine
Unlike valproate and carbamazepine, lamotrigine carries no risks at all
The risks of lamotrigine are equivalent to those of valproate and carbamazepine
Lamotrigine is safer in pregnancy than carbamazepine or valproate

correct_answer.text: Lamotrigine is safer in pregnancy than carbamazepine or valproate

correct_answers.text: Lamotrigine is safer in pregnancy than carbamazepine or valproate

questions.explanation: There is growing evidence that lamotrigine is safer in pregnancy than carbamazepine or valproate across a range of outcomes. The risk of major malformations with lamotrigine appears to be in the range reported for children not exposed to anticonvulsants. Behaviour problems have been reported by parents of children exposed to lamotrigine in pregnancy. Lamotrigine may be associated with an increased risk of autism. Clearance of lamotrigine seems to increase radically during pregnancy and then reduces postpartum. NICE advises that if a pregnant woman is taking lamotrigine, lamotrigine levels should be checked frequently during pregnancy and into the postnatal period because they vary substantially. Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 691-692.

questions.question_text: The core symptom of myalgic encephalomyelitis is
questions.explanation: Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) is a clinical syndrome, the central feature of which is severe fatigue, unrelated to exertion or triggered only by minimal activity, and unrelieved by rest. The fatigue is experienced as a subjective feeling of lethargy, lack of energy, exhaustion, and a feeling of 'increased effort to do anything'. Patients also often complain of aching muscles, sleep disturbance, aching joints, headaches, and difficulties with concentration. They may date the onset of symptoms very precisely to an episode of viral infection with sore throat, fever, and tender lymph nodes. The syndrome was previously referred to as neurasthenia, then as myalgic encephalomyelitis. The term CFS was later preferred, as it did not imply knowledge of underlying pathology or aetiology. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 874.

questions.question_text: Mr. Q suffers from epilepsy and psychosis with paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations. He is worried about metabolic side effects of newer antipsychotics and would like to take an older antipsychotic medication. Of the following, the drug that should be avoided in his case would be
questions.explanation: Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 790.
